chapter: Hollywood, Ken Murray and the Penguin years
title: Sonora records and the mix of singing and solos
summary: Criticized for too little playing, he praises the Sonora sides and says Dresnon was more father than manager.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: On that Sonora, they really--the Man With The Funny Horn was very good, but on the Sonora records--you ought to hear them. Do you have time for me to play them?
Oh, sure.
I want you to hear the execution of the things I did in Social Drag and You Went Too Far and Stayed Too Long.
Who was Sonora; who was that?
It was a big company that had a few million dollars that they just signed up too many people.
Who was recording it for you?
Quite a few; Georgie
Gibbs--
No, I mean who was recording you? Who was the guy that signed you at Sonora?
This was the president of the company; I forget her name.
It was a woman?
A woman, yeah. She got in touch with me. In fact, I guess she looked in the phone book; she sent me this letter to please get in touch.
In the meantime, Dresnon didn't mind it because this is during the time that you were recording for him, for Penguin?
Right.
Did he realize that he could not get that much business on his own label?
That's right.
So he said okay.
That's the reason why I said he was more of a father than a manager.
Because he didn't mind;
No, it didn't bother him at all.
Was he supervising the sessions as well or was somebody else actually in the studio?
I supervised it. He was there but--
